title: PORNOGRAPHY, OBJECTIFICATION, AND JESUS’ TERRIFYING WARNING ABOUT THE EYES
paragraphs: PORNOGRAPHY, OBJECTIFICATION, AND JESUS’ TERRIFYING WARNING ABOUT THE EYES

The screen goes dark. The history gets deleted. Nobody in the house knows. But Jesus said the real battle was never merely on the screen—it was happening somewhere no browser can hide: inside the heart.
There is a moment after pornography that almost nobody talks about.
The screen goes dark.
The room becomes quiet again.
Whatever excitement existed seconds earlier begins collapsing into something heavier.
You close the tab.
Delete the history.
Maybe clear the search bar.
Maybe put the phone facedown beside you.
And for a few seconds, you just lie there.
Alone.
Maybe ashamed.
Maybe numb.
Maybe promising God for the hundredth time that this really was the last time.
“Lord, forgive me.”
You mean it.
At least you think you mean it.
Then tomorrow comes.
Or three days.
Or two weeks.
And somehow your hand finds the phone again.
Your eyes begin wandering again.
The private negotiation begins again.
Just one look.
I won't go further.
Nobody knows.
I'm not actually touching anyone.
I'm not cheating physically.
It's only a screen.
Then the words of Jesus enter the room.
And suddenly all the excuses become very quiet.

“You have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.” — Matthew 5:27–28, KJV
Read the words beneath the English.
The Greek of Matthew 5:28 says:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
The force of the sentence matters.

Jesus is not teaching that noticing an attractive person is identical to adultery. He is not declaring that involuntary temptation itself is the completed sin. He is describing the gaze directed toward lust—the looking that welcomes desire, cultivates it, feeds it, and turns another human being into material for inward sexual possession.
That distinction matters because some tender consciences have been crushed by the idea that simply noticing beauty means they have already committed adultery.
That is not what Jesus is teaching.
But the other distortion is just as dangerous.
Some people use that distinction to excuse the second look.
And the third.
And the search.
And the fantasy.
And the saved video.
And the secret account.
And the midnight scrolling.
Jesus refuses both errors.
He does not condemn you merely for having eyes.
He confronts what your heart decides to do with what your eyes see.
And pornography is almost perfectly engineered around the very thing Jesus exposes.
The prolonged gaze.
The intentionally cultivated desire.
The consumption of another person's body for personal gratification.
Pornography whispers, “Look longer.”
Jesus asks what the looking is doing to your heart.
Pornography says, “They're only bodies.”
Jesus reveals people as human beings made by God, never commodities created for our consumption.
Pornography trains the imagination to ask, “What can this body give me?”
Christ teaches us to ask, “How can I love my neighbor?”
That is why objectification is not a small side effect of pornography.
It is woven into its logic.
A person becomes an image.
An image becomes stimulation.
Stimulation becomes consumption.
Consumption demands novelty.
And somewhere along that road, the human being on the screen becomes easier to forget.
She has a name.
He has a name.
They have histories.
Parents.
Wounds.
Fears.
Souls.
They bear the dignity belonging to human creatures made in God's image.
Yet lust can train the heart to stop seeing a person and start seeing parts.
And Jesus takes that seriously enough to say something terrifying immediately after His warning about lust.
“If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee…”
Matthew 5:29.
The Greek is startling:
“εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε…”
ei de ho ophthalmos sou ho dexios skandalizei se…
“If your right eye causes you to stumble…”
Then:
“ἔξελε αὐτὸν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ…”
Take it away.
Cast it from you.
Jesus continues with the right hand.
Cut it off.
Throw it away.
This is deliberately shocking language.

But Jesus is not commanding His followers to mutilate their bodies. Removing an eye cannot remove lust from the heart. A blind person can still fantasize. Removing a hand cannot amputate sinful desire from the soul.
Jesus has already located the battlefield.
“ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
En tē kardia autou.
“In his heart.”
That is where the war is.
The eye may become a doorway.
The hand may become an instrument.
The phone may become an access point.
The browser may become a hiding place.
But the heart is where sin must ultimately be confronted.
Jesus' violent imagery communicates something modern Christianity can become dangerously reluctant to say:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Some things should not be managed.
They should be removed.
Some doors should not merely be resisted.
They should be locked.
Some accounts should not merely be visited less frequently.
They should be deleted.
Some apps should disappear.
Some private browsing habits need to end.
Some phones need restrictions.
Some passwords need to belong to an accountability partner.
Some late-night routines need to change.
Some friendships need enough honesty for you finally to say:
“I need help.”
Because there comes a point when saying, “I'm praying about it,” while protecting unrestricted access to the very thing feeding the sin becomes spiritual contradiction.
Prayer is not supposed to become camouflage for refusing obedience.
Imagine someone standing inside a burning house praying for God to save him while refusing to walk through the open door.
Sometimes God's answer to your prayer for freedom looks painfully practical.
Delete it.
Block it.
Confess it.
Leave the room.
Call someone.
Stop carrying your phone into bed.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Run.
Paul's instruction concerning sexual immorality was not, “Study how close you can stand to it.”
“Flee fornication.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18, KJV
Flee.
There is movement in that word.
Joseph understood this long before smartphones existed.
Potiphar's wife offered secrecy, access, opportunity, and sexual temptation.
Joseph did not remain in the room to demonstrate how spiritually mature he was.
He ran.
He left his garment behind.
Sometimes victory looks less impressive than we imagined.
Sometimes victory is simply getting out of the room.
But pornography has another lie.
It tells you that because you have returned so many times, you are probably beyond restoration.
That lie has buried people almost as deeply as lust itself.
Because after repeated failure, shame begins preaching.
“You're disgusting.”
“You aren't a real Christian.”
“God must be tired of you.”
“Don't tell anybody.”
“Hide.”
And hiding is exactly where bondage grows best.
Remember the first human response after sin entered the world.
Adam and Eve hid.
Sin produced shame.
Shame produced hiding.
And God came looking.
“Where art thou?” — Genesis 3:9.
Not because God lacked information.
The question exposed the distance sin had created.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide behind humor.
Behind ministry.
Behind marriages.
Behind church attendance.
Behind deleted histories.
Behind Bible verses.
Behind worship playlists.
Behind the phrase, “I'm doing okay.”
And sometimes the person singing loudest on Sunday night is fighting a war nobody knows about by midnight.
Maybe that's you.
Maybe nobody knows how tired you are.
Maybe you've confessed the same sin to God so many times that even the words feel worn out.
Maybe you have wondered whether repentance still counts when you have failed again.
Hear this carefully.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the announcement that chains do not have to remain your master.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become comfortable with the darkness.
He shed His blood to redeem sinners from it.
The Gospel does not say sexual sin is insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required the death of the Son of God.
But grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly came.
Jesus knew what humanity had done.
He knew what humanity would do.
He knew every hidden browser.
Every affair.
Every fantasy.
Every secret addiction.
Every objectifying gaze.
Every relapse.
Every lie told to cover another lie.
And Christ still went toward Calvary.
Not because sin was harmless.
Because love was costly.
There the sinless Christ bore judgment for sinners.
There mercy and justice met.
There forgiveness was purchased not by our promises to improve but by His finished work.
And there is something pornography can never give you that Jesus freely offers.
To be completely known...
and still invited home.
Pornography offers exposure without intimacy.
Christ offers intimacy without exploitation.
Pornography says, “Consume.”
Jesus says, “Love.”
Pornography says, “Use.”
Jesus says, “Serve.”
Pornography says, “Take.”
Jesus gave Himself.
Pornography teaches you to detach someone's body from covenant, responsibility, sacrifice, and personhood.
The Gospel reveals a Savior whose love is demonstrated precisely through sacrifice.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Look at the contrast.
Lust asks:
What can I take from you?
Christlike love asks:
What can I give for you?
That is why freedom from pornography is not merely about becoming better at saying no.
It is about learning to see again.
Seeing women as image-bearers rather than images.
Seeing men as image-bearers rather than bodies.
Seeing sexuality as God's gift rather than our god.
Seeing marriage as covenant rather than consumption.
Seeing singleness as a life capable of holiness and fullness rather than a waiting room for sexual fulfillment.
Seeing your own body not as an appetite demanding obedience but as belonging to the Lord.
Paul writes:
Bought with a price.
That changes the question.
The Christian no longer asks only:
“Can I get away with this?”
We begin asking:
“Does this belong in a life purchased by Jesus Christ?”
And perhaps that question hurts.
Good.
Not because God delights in humiliating you.
Because conviction can be mercy.
The surgeon's warning sounds frightening when the disease is serious.
Jesus speaks fiercely because eternity matters.
He loves us too much to call slavery freedom.
And His warning in Matthew 5 does not stop with the eye.
Jesus speaks of Gehenna.
Judgment.
The stakes are eternal.
That truth should sober every one of us.
Christianity is not behavior modification with inspirational music.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance, faith, and a transformed life.
Yet we must never reverse the Gospel.
You do not defeat pornography so that Jesus will finally love you.
You come to Jesus because sinners cannot rescue themselves.
You do not cleanse yourself sufficiently and then approach Christ.
You approach Christ for cleansing.
You do not earn the cross.
You collapse beneath it.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV.
Notice the Gospel does not tell us to pretend.
Confess.
The Greek word commonly translated “confess” in that verse is homologeō—to acknowledge, to say the same thing, to agree.
Stop renaming what God has named.
Stop calling bondage “just a habit.”
Stop calling lust “appreciating beauty.”
Stop calling secrecy “privacy” when secrecy exists specifically to protect sin.
Stop promising tomorrow what obedience requires today.
Bring it into the light.
And if you fall?
Do not turn failure into permission to surrender.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Get up.
Remove access.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Fight again.
Not because repeated sin does not matter.
Because Jesus is still worthy of the fight.
Some people reading this have been fighting pornography for years.
Others clicked something for the first time recently and already feel the hook.
Some are husbands hiding it from wives.
Some are wives hiding it from husbands.
Some are teenagers terrified that their parents will discover their history.
Some are pastors.
Some are worship leaders.
Some are people who have never told another human being.
And some are reading this while carrying wounds connected to being objectified themselves.
If that is you, understand this:
Jesus does not look at you the way pornography does.
He does not reduce you to your body.
He does not measure your worth by desirability.
He does not consume you.
He knows you.
Your body is not merchandise.
Your dignity is not determined by somebody else's lust.
Your value is not established by whether somebody wants your body.
You were made by God.
And for those who have spent years objectifying others, repentance includes learning to recognize that dignity again.
The person on the screen is not pixels.
The woman walking past you is not a fantasy.
The man at the gym is not material for your imagination.
Look differently.
Not fearfully.
Not awkwardly.
Not with contempt for human beauty.
With holiness.
With love.
With honor.
Because purity is not learning to hate bodies.
God created bodies.
Christian purity is learning to refuse the lie that another person's body exists for your unauthorized consumption.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that pornography shocks you anymore.
Perhaps it is that it doesn't.
Things that once disturbed you can slowly become normal.
What once required searching becomes scrolling.
What once produced immediate conviction begins producing excuses.
What once made you weep before God becomes something you casually promise to deal with later.
That is why Jesus' words must remain sharp.
Not because Christ wants wounded sinners terrified to approach Him.
Because He refuses to let comfortable sinners sleep peacefully while walking toward destruction.
Wake up.
There is still grace.
There is still a cross.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still repentance.
There is still resurrection power.
There is still a Savior who receives sinners.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus and became a preacher of Christ.
The Corinthian church included people rescued from profound sexual sin, and Paul could write:
Were.
That word is beautiful.
Your sin may explain part of your history.
It does not have to dictate your destiny.
This is the scandal of grace.
Christ does not merely improve respectable people.
He resurrects sinners.
He enters stories we would rather delete and begins writing redemption across pages covered in shame.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So tonight, before you reach for the phone, remember whose eyes you have.
Before you search, remember whose body you belong to.
Before you hide, remember that Christ already knows.
Before shame convinces you to run away from Jesus, run toward Him.
And if something keeps dragging you back into darkness, take His warning seriously enough to become radical.
Not self-mutilation.
Surrender.
Remove access.
Destroy secrecy.
Confess the sin.
Seek trustworthy Christian accountability.
If necessary, seek qualified professional help alongside pastoral care, especially where compulsive behavior, trauma, or severe relational damage is involved.
Do whatever righteous wisdom requires to stop feeding what is trying to master you.
Your eye is not your master.
Your appetite is not your master.
Pornography is not your master.
If you belong to Christ, Jesus is Lord.
Maybe this article exposed something you have hidden for years.
Be honest.
If secrecy has been poisoning you and today you are choosing the light, comment, “No more hiding.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if Jesus has already begun restoring what sexual sin damaged, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading your three words may realize they are not the only person fighting.
That matters.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money purchases blessing. It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be bought.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it. If you want to glorify God through what He has entrusted to you, one legitimate expression of stewardship is helping faithful Gospel resources continue to be created, distributed, shared, and placed before people who might otherwise never encounter them.
Send it privately to the person God just brought to your mind.
Because perhaps somewhere tonight...
another room is dark.
Another phone is glowing.
Another person is seconds away from surrendering again.
And perhaps your share will place one sentence in front of them before temptation does.
Maybe they will stop.
Maybe they will pray.
Maybe they will confess.
Maybe they will finally ask for help.
Maybe they will discover that Jesus is not standing at the end of repentance with crossed arms.
He is the reason repentance can lead home.
And maybe years from now, they will barely remember the image they almost clicked...
but they will remember the night Christ interrupted them.
The screen can be turned off in a second—but only Jesus can teach the heart to see a human being again.
